pmt3.name: Low-background 3-inch PMTs
refs: Composition: Hamamatsu R11410MOD materials per tube (Hamamatsu Photonics, 'Development of PMT (R11410MOD) for Dark Matter Experiment', 2010): quartz faceplate 35 g, Kovar body 95 g, ceramic stem 25 g, insulating plates 16 g (171 g in all; the plates are treated as ceramic). Kovar taken as 53.5% Fe, 29% Ni, 17% Co (nominal).

Radioactivity per tube quoted by the manufacturer for the R11410-10 (3.3 mBq ²³⁸U, 2.3 mBq ²³²Th, 5.7 mBq ⁴⁰K, 9.1 mBq ⁶⁰Co): K. Lung et al., arXiv:1202.2628; divided by 0.171 kg per tube, chains assumed in equilibrium. Screened production tubes for recent experiments are often cleaner.
Underground thermal flux 1.08×10⁻⁶ n cm⁻² s⁻¹: P. Belli et al., Il Nuovo Cimento A 101 (1989) 959 (Gran Sasso).
Underground fast flux ≈ 0.9×10⁻⁷ n cm⁻² s⁻¹ (Gran Sasso), as summarized in R. Bernabei et al., arXiv:1409.3516.

Surface fast flux (> 1 MeV) 5.5×10⁻³ n cm⁻² s⁻¹: integral of the sea-level spectrum parameterization of M.S. Gordon et al., IEEE Trans. Nucl. Sci. 51 (2004) 3427 (it gives 13 n cm⁻² h⁻¹ above 10 MeV). The surface thermal flux is assumed equal to it (no evaluated default; enter a measured value if you have one).

presets.name: DarkSide-50 (LAr TPC)
notes: All components sit within ~10 cm of the active argon; their full masses are used.
Steel: cryostat body 142 kg, flanges 30.0 kg, organ-pipe tubes, bolts, nuts, washers, grid and grid ring (178.6 kg).
PTFE: support structures 35.88 kg + reflector 22.34 kg. Copper: field-cage rings 16.5 kg + PMT screws 0.887 kg.
PMTs: 38 Hamamatsu R11065 (Kovar shells 5.31 kg in all), entered as 38 × 0.171 kg low-background 3-inch PMTs.
Polyethylene: multilayer-insulation netting 1.04 kg. Solder: 0.050 kg.

Left out: fused-silica windows and diving bell (3.2 kg; much cleaner than the borosilicate glass in this tool), the 30 t liquid-scintillator veto and 1 kt water tank (very radiopure liquids that also shield the rock: rock set to 0).
refs: S.S. Westerdale, "A Study of Nuclear Recoil Backgrounds in Dark Matter Detectors", PhD thesis, Princeton University (2016), FERMILAB-THESIS-2016-39, Tables 2.1–2.2 (DarkSide-50 TPC components).

presets.name: DEAP-3600 (single-phase LAr)

PMTs: 255 R5912 PMTs, 516 kg (mostly borosilicate glass), × 0.037 for 50 cm of acrylic in front of them.
Steel: 3.4 m shell, 5012 kg (≈ 1.7 cm thick), × 0.027.
Liquid argon: 3279 kg. Rock: 0 (inside a 7.8 m water tank). Polyurethane foam (~80 kg, behind the PMTs) left out.
refs: R. Ajaj et al. (DEAP Collaboration), "Electromagnetic backgrounds and potassium-42 activity in the DEAP-3600 dark matter detector", Phys. Rev. D 100 (2019) 072009, doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.100.072009, Tables V–VI (component masses).

P.-A. Amaudruz et al. (DEAP Collaboration), "Design and construction of the DEAP-3600 dark matter detector", Astropart. Phys. 108 (2019) 1, doi:10.1016/j.astropartphys.2018.09.006 (geometry: 5 cm acrylic vessel, 45 cm light guides, 3.4 m steel shell, LAr mass).

Attenuation lengths at 1.5 MeV: Klein–Nishina Compton cross section (Cu 2.37 cm, steel 2.63 cm, acrylic 15.2 cm, polyethylene 17.9 cm, LAB scintillator 20.1 cm) and the NIST XCOM total for lead (0.0522 cm²/g, 1.69 cm): M.J. S.name: ¹H(n,γ)²H
S.how: Thermal-neutron capture on ¹H (99.99% of natural hydrogen, σ ≈ 0.333 b): 100.0% of captures in natural hydrogen. The compound nucleus ²H emits ≈ 1.0 gammas per capture (separation energy 2225 keV).
S.where: Anywhere hydrogen sits in a thermal neutron flux. Present in: polyethylene, borated polyethylene, water, rock/concrete, acrylic.
tests: The 2223 keV line follows the thermal neutron flux in hydrogenous material (water, polyethylene, people, scintillator).
No coincident gamma: a single line per capture.
Delayed by ~200 µs after a neutron enters water or scintillator (thermalisation and capture time).
S.unit: Intensity: gammas per 100 captures on ¹H.

S.name: ¹⁰⁰Mo(n,n′γ)¹⁰⁰Mo
S.how: Fast neutrons (from (α,n) reactions and fission in rock, and from cosmic-ray muons) excite low-lying levels of ¹⁰⁰Mo (9.744% of natural molybdenum), which emit these gammas.
S.where: Anywhere molybdenum sees fast neutrons. Present in: steel.
tests: Rate follows the fast neutron flux; moderators reduce it, boron does not.
Lines from the first excited state are the strongest; higher levels need faster neutrons.
Inside a germanium or argon target the recoiling nucleus adds energy, giving an asymmetric tail to higher energy.
S.unit: Relative weights only (strongest = 100), from each level's gamma branching and a factor favouring low-lying levels. For ranking, a total gamma-production cross section of 1 b per nucleus is assumed and shared by these weights; real strengths depend on the neutron spectrum and on per-level cross sections, which are not yet included.
refs: Level energies and gamma branching (adopted levels of ¹⁰⁰Mo): ENSDF evaluation by Balraj Singh, Jun Chen (literature cut-off 31-Jan-2021), retrieved from the IAEA LiveChart of Nuclides 2026-11-23.

S.name: ²⁷Al(α,p)³⁰Si
S.how: Alphas from uranium- and thorium-chain contaminants and ²¹⁰Po inside the material hit ²⁷Al nuclei (100% of natural aluminum). The ²⁷Al(α,p)³⁰Si reaction leaves ³⁰Si in excited states, which emit these gammas at once.
S.where: Materials containing aluminum with alpha-emitting contamination: aluminium, rock/concrete, borosilicate glass, low-background PMTs.
tests: Rate follows the material's alpha activity (²¹⁰Po, radon progeny, U/Th chains), not the neutron flux: shielding does not change it.
Lines from light nuclei are Doppler-broadened: the residual nucleus recoils fast and often decays in flight.
The same reaction may also emit a neutron; check the other lines from this target.
S.unit: Intensity: share of this reaction's gammas (%%, weighted over typical materials). Rates: thick-target yields for alphas stopping in each material, times that material's chain activities.
refs: Gamma-production cross sections σγ(Eα): TALYS-1.95 (A.J. Koning & D. Rochman, Nucl. Data Sheets 113 (2012) 2841, doi:10.1016/j.nds.2012.11.002), as tabulated in the NeuCBOT datasets (github.com/neucbot-datasets).
Thick-target yield method, alpha spectra (from ENSDF) and stopping-power tables: NeuCBOT (S. Westerdale & P.D. Meyers, Nucl. Instrum. Meth. A 875 (2017) 57, doi:10.1016/j.nima.2017.09.007).

S.name: ⁵⁰Ti(α,n)⁵³Cr
S.how: Alphas from uranium- and thorium-chain contaminants and ²¹⁰Po inside the material hit ⁵⁰Ti nuclei (5.18% of natural titanium). The ⁵⁰Ti(α,n)⁵³Cr reaction leaves ⁵³Cr in excited states, which emit these gammas at once.
S.where: Materials containing titanium with alpha-emitting contamination: titanium, rock/concrete.
tests: Rate follows the material's alpha activity (²¹⁰Po, radon progeny, U/Th chains), not the neutron flux: shielding does not change it.
Lines from light nuclei are Doppler-broadened: the residual nucleus recoils fast and often decays in flight.
The same reaction may also emit a neutron (it is an (α,n) reaction), so look for capture or inelastic lines too.

S.name: Annihilation (e⁺e⁻ → γγ)
S.how: Positrons from β⁺ decays, pair production by high-energy gammas and cosmic-ray muon showers.
S.where: Every detector; strongest at the surface and near β⁺ emitters (²²Na, ⁶⁸Ga, ⁵⁸Co, ⁶⁵Zn, ²⁶Al, ¹⁸F, ⁴⁸V).
tests: The 511 keV peak is broader than nearby lines (Doppler broadening of positronium/positrons).
Falls sharply underground and with veto-tagged muons removed.

S.unit: Relative intensities.

refs: ⁷Li 477.6 keV level: ENSDF (adopted levels of ⁷Li).
Branching (≈94% of thermal ¹⁰B(n,α) reactions populate the 478 keV state): ENDF/B-VIII.0 (D.A. Brown et al., Nucl. Data Sheets 148 (2018) 1).
Rate: ¹⁰B abundance 19.65% (IAEA LiveChart) and thermal absorption cross section 3835 b (Rauch & Waschkowski 2003).
S.unit: Intensity: gammas per 100 ¹⁰B(n,α) reactions.
S.name: ¹⁰B(n,α)⁷Li*
S.how: Thermal neutron capture on boron: 94% of captures leave ⁷Li in its 478 keV state.
S.where: Borated polyethylene shielding, boron-loaded rubber, borosilicate glass, Pyrex.
tests: Strongly Doppler-broadened (several keV) because the ⁷Li recoils in flight.
Scales with the thermal neutron flux; grows with more borated material nearby.
No other gamma from the same reaction: the α particle and ⁷Li stay inside the material.

refs: ⁷²Ge 691.4 keV 0⁺ level (E0 decay): ENSDF (adopted levels of ⁷²Ge).
For ranking, an excitation cross section of 0.1 b is assumed (order of magnitude; not evaluated).
S.unit: Single feature; no gamma is emitted (conversion electrons only).
S.name: ⁷²Ge(n,n′) 0⁺ state (E0)
S.how: Fast neutrons excite ⁷²Ge's first excited 0⁺ state inside a germanium detector; it decays by conversion electrons, not a gamma.
S.where: Germanium detectors only.
tests: Peak has a sharp left edge and a tail to higher energy: the germanium recoil energy adds to the 691 keV deposit.
Seen only when the excitation happens inside the germanium crystal itself.
Scales with the fast neutron flux, like ⁷⁴Ge(n,n′) at 596 keV.

refs: ⁷⁴Ge 595.85 keV level: ENSDF (adopted levels of ⁷⁴Ge).
For ranking, an excitation cross section of 0.5 b is assumed (order of magnitude; not evaluated).
S.unit: Single feature.
S.name: ⁷⁴Ge(n,n′γ) in the detector
S.how: Fast neutrons excite ⁷⁴Ge's 596 keV level inside a germanium detector.
S.where: Germanium detectors only.
tests: Asymmetric 'triangle' peak: the germanium recoil energy is summed with the 596 keV gamma.
Compare with 691 keV (⁷²Ge 0⁺): both scale with the fast neutron flux.
A symmetric 596 keV peak instead points to ⁷³Ge(n,γ) capture or ⁷⁴As decay.

S.name: ⁹Be(α,n)¹²C*

tests: Doppler-broadened by tens of keV.

Strong near reactors' cooling water.
